newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's right wing comes unglued.
newsitem.headline: Israel's right wing comes unglued.

text.p: When Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu forged his first peace deal with the Arabs on Hebron last week, his right-wing power base in Israel came unglued.

Jewish settlers who had viewed the Likud party leader as a Godsend rent their clothes. His cabinet split 11-7 on the accord. Science Minister Binyamin Begin, son of Likud founder Menachem Begin, quit his job.

Hardliners accused Netanyahu of betraying them by negotiating with the PLO's Yasser Arafat, long branded a terrorist, and ceding part of Hebron, a sacred West Bank town they view as part of "Greater Israel" God gave the Jews.

It made no difference that Netanyahu had begrudgingly sealed the agreement, heaping yet more scorn on the Oslo peace process he inherited with his election in May, or that Netanyahu's negotiator signed the deal behind closed doors.

Some were asking why they had even bothered to back the 47-year-old Netanyahu, a relative political newcomer who defeated the Nobel peace laureate, Labour party prime minister Shimon Peres, by fewer than 30,000 votes.
"It leaves the right wing in a state of split -- the ideological hardcore and the more pragmatic one," said a senior Likud activist who spoke on condition he not be identified.

So long as Netanyahu sticks to a promise -- proven popular with the Israeli electorate -- to abide by international commitments and pursue peacemaking, the hardcore minority will soon find itself without an agenda, the activist said.
"I think you have to redefine the right-wing," said Israeli political philosopher Meron Benvenisti.

"The old definition of 'right-wing' equals 'anti-PLO', 'Greater Israel' is no longer relevant. I think that you have a much more sophisticated approach to those issues and they're non-ideological," he told Reuters.

The Israeli right helped Netanyahu win the election. But so did the Israeli middle -- those floating voters won over by Netanyahu's dual promises to halt suicide bombers and make a better peace -- brought him to power.
"We needed the votes of the centre -- otherwise we would not have won the election," said the activist.
Despite conventional wisdom Netanyahu was feeling pressure from Washington to close a deal, Likud activists said there was no less pressure from within Israel itself.
A Gallup poll of 509 Israeli Jews last week showed 57 percent backed the Hebron deal. Only 19 percent opposed it. The rest had no opinion.

The 70 percent majority Netanyahu's deal got in parliament, built on all but the hardline right, would have been the envy of late Labour Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin whose breakthrough PLO peace deals passed by paper-thin majorities.

Even after Netanyahu opened a pedestrian tourist tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem in September, sparking violence that claimed the lives of 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis, nearly 80 percent of Israelis said they wanted to press ahead with peace moves.

Trade Minister Natan Sharansky, who wavered on the deal before finally casting his lot with Netanyahu during a 12-hour cabinet debate, said Zionists left and right had to feel some sadness about giving up part of their historic homeland.
"But idealism must be joined with pragmatism," he wrote on Sunday in the newspaper Haaretz.

"There are more than 100,000 Palestinians living in Hebron today and we must ensure them a maximal ability to run their own lives and at the same time provide maximum possible security for the (400) Jewish residents," he continued.

Whatever lies ahead with the Palestinians, the Israeli political right faces a stormy future as it goes on redefining itself. Netanyahu himself may have given in on Hebron, but his Land of Israel ideology will still guide peace moves.
Jewish settlers will likely demand -- and get -- Netanyahu's support to expand their West Bank enclaves.

Hawkish cabinet minister Ariel Sharon will push for a national unity government with Peres, hoping to enhance a political role diminished by a new electoral system that sapped ministers like himself of powers they had in previous cabinets.
Meanwhile members of parliament from Likud and Labour are drafting a paper meant to coalesce a consensus for the two main parties on future negotiations with the Palestinians.
"We are in for troubles. We are in for a stormy period," said the Likud activist. "We are in for a difficult period because we are about to make crucial historic decisions."
